evildoer.e: From Middle English yvel doer; equivalent to evil + doer.

d.g: An evil or wicked act, especially a crime.
The quality or state of being evil.

evilness.e: From Middle English yvelnesse, from Old English yfelnyss; equivalent to evil + -ness.

d.g: A disemboweling; the removal of viscera.
d.x: The evisceration of the animal was accomplished with a single blow of the knife.

d.g: A vigorous verbal or physical assault.
d.x: The critic delivered another evisceration of the latest movie.

d.g: The act of calling out or forth, or evoking.
d.x: a stunningly atmospheric evocation of urban ennui

d.g: A manoeuvre of troops or ships.
d.x: Major Holroyd, who acted as the General, was extremely polite, and attentive, and came to us between every evolution, to explain and talk over the manoeuvres.

d.g: A turning movement, especially of the body.
d.x: It was a critical instant: the pirouette -- it would fail, she feared. … the rapid whirl achieved in exact time, the whole evolution executed to perfection.

d.g: The opening out of a curve; now more generally, the gradual transformation of a curve by a change of the conditions generating it.
The extraction of a root from a given power.

evolution.e: Borrowed from Latin ēvolūtiō, ēvolūtiōnis (“the act of unrolling, unfolding or opening (of a book)”), from ēvolūtus, perfect passive participle of ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ex + volvō (“roll”). …

d.g: Any of several theories that explain the evolution of systems or organisms.
The belief in the universal presence of evolution.
The advocacy of Darwinian evolution by natural selection (Darwinism).

evolutionism.e: English evolution Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Indo-European *-mos Proto-Indo-European *-mós Ancient Greek -μός (-mós) Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós)der. English -ism English evolutionism From evolution + -ism.

d.g: A proponent or supporter of evolutionism.
Someone who believes in the capacity of people to change.
d.x: Aeschylus is in fact an evolutionist as regards both gods and man.

evolutionist.e: English evolution Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō) Proto-Hellenic *-tās Ancient Greek -τής (-tḗs) Ancient Greek -ῐστής (-ĭstḗs)bor. Latin -istader. Old French -istebor. …

d.g: To leave or withdraw from; to quit; to retire from.
d.x: The soldiers evacuated the fortress.

d.g: To cause (or help) to leave or withdraw from.
d.x: The firefighters decided to evacuate all the inhabitants from the street.

d.g: To make empty; to empty out; to remove the contents of, including to create a vacuum.
d.x: The scientist evacuated the chamber before filling it with nitrogen.

d.g: To make empty; to deprive.
d.x: Evacuate the Scriptures of their most important doctrines.

evacuate.e: First attested in 1526; borrowed from Latin ēvacuātus, the perfect passive participle of ēvacuō (“to empty out, evacuate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

d.g: To get away from by cunning; to avoid by using dexterity, subterfuge, address, or ingenuity; to cleverly escape from.
d.x: He evaded his opponent's blows.

d.g: To escape; to slip away; — sometimes with from.
d.x: Evading from perils.

d.g: To attempt to escape; to practice artifice or sophistry, for the purpose of eluding.
d.x: The ministers of God are not to evade and take refuge any of these ... ways.

evade.e: From Middle French évader, from Latin ēvādō (“to pass or go over; flee”), from ē (“out of, from”) + vādō (“to go; walk”). See also wade.

d.g: To draw conclusions from examining; to assess; to appraise.
d.x: It will take several years to evaluate the material gathered in the survey.

d.g: To compute or determine the value of (an expression).
d.x: Evaluate this integral.

d.g: To return or have a specific value.
To disappear into a mist or dissipate in vapor
d.x: All his cares evanesced.

d.g: To transition from the solid state to gaseous state without ever becoming a liquid

evanesce.e: From Latin evanescere (“to vanish”). Doublet of vanish.

d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of evangelize.

evangelise.e: From Old French évangéliser, equivalent to evangel + -ise.

d.g: To tell people about (a particular branch of) Christianity, especially in order to convert them; to preach the gospel to.
d.x: his Apoſtles, whom he ſends To evangelize the Nations

d.g: To preach any ideology to those who have not yet been converted to it.
d.x: […] nor is it the task of the Muslim to "evangelize" the unbelieving world.

d.g: To be enthusiastic about something, and to attempt to share that enthusiasm with others; to promote.

evangelize.e: From Old French évangéliser, equivalent to evangel + -ize, from Late Latin evangelizare, from Ancient Greek εὐαγγελίζω (euangelízō). Displaced native Old English godspellian (literally “to gospel”).

d.g: To transition from a liquid state into a gaseous state.
To expel moisture from (usually by means of artificial heat), leaving the solid portion.
d.x: to evaporate apples

d.g: To give vent to; to dissipate.
d.x: [M]y lord of Eſſex choſe to evaporate his thoughts in a Sonnet (being his common vvay) to be ſung before the Queen, […]

d.g: To disappear; to escape or pass off without effect.
d.x: Near-synonym: go up in smoke

evaporate.e: First attested in 1545, borrowed from Latin ēvapōrātus, the perfect passive participle of ēvapōrō (“to evaporate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix). …

d.g: To have a given result; to turn out (well, badly etc.); to result in.
d.x: Enoch Powell appeared to insult the memory of Dr. King by making a speech warning that “colored” immigration to Britain would eventuate in bloodshed.

d.g: To happen as a result; to come about.
d.x: Reconciliation cannot eventuate or materialise until the proper legal procedures have been followed, that is without interference from external forces.

eventuate.e: American English, from Latin ēventu(s) (“an event, happening”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix), perhaps modeled after actuate.

d.g: To expel (one or more people) from their property; to force (one or more people) to move out.
d.x: evict a tenant

d.g: To eject from a memory cache to reduce the cache's size.

evict.e: From Middle English evicten, evycten, borrowed from Latin ēvictus, past participle of ēvincō (“to vanquish completely”). Doublet of evince.

d.g: To show or demonstrate clearly; to manifest.
d.x: Common sense and experience will and must evince the truth of this.

evince.e: From Middle French évincer, from Latin ēvincō (“conquer entirely, prevail over; prove exhaustively”), from ē- (short form of ex- (intensive prefix)) + vincō (“conquer”). Doublet of evict.

d.g: To call out; to draw out or bring forth.
To cause the manifestation of something (emotion, picture, etc.) in someone's mind or imagination.
d.x: Being here evokes long forgotten memories.

d.g: To elicit a response.

evoke.e: From French évoquer, from Latin ēvocō (“to call out, summon”), from ex (“out”) and vocō (“call”). Akin to voice.

d.g: To move (something) in regular procession through a system.
d.x: The animal soul sooner expands and evolves it self to its full orb and extent than the humane Soul

d.g: To change or transform (something).
d.x: Over several years the author evolved the story originally drafted as a novella into a real epic.

d.g: To cause (something) to come into being or develop.
d.x: You will remove the pig, place it in the car, and drive it to my house in Wiltshire. That is the plan I have evolved.

d.g: Of a population: to acquire or develop (a trait) in the process of biological evolution.
d.x: How long ago did birds evolve beaks?

evolve.e: Borrowed from Latin ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ē- (“out of”) (short form of ex) + volvō (“roll”).
